This tutorial first explains the role of a subunit and presents the bundled
model catalogue. You will then define a flexible linker without writing C++,
validate it, use it in a coated-particle model, save and reload the topology,
evaluate its form factor, and export a deterministic 3D realization.

## What is a subunit?

A subunit is a reusable scattering component. It supplies its normalized form
factor, amplitudes relative to its reference points, phase factors between
those references, structural parameters, and size measures. pySEB connects
subunits through specific references such as a polymer end or sphere center,
or distributed references such as a contour or surface.

Subunits describe local scattering physics. A `World` supplies instance names,
parameter-sharing tags, links, and reusable nested structures. Keeping those
responsibilities separate lets one subunit definition participate in chains,
stars, micelles, dendrimers, and other composite models.

## Explore the bundled subunits

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

from _helpers import (
    bundled_subunit_catalogue,
    bundled_subunit_figure,
    bundled_subunit_markdown,
)

catalogue = bundled_subunit_catalogue()
print(bundled_subunit_markdown(catalogue))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-bundled-subunit-catalogue
#| fig-cap: "Bundled YAML subunits rendered automatically from their OpenUSD visualization definitions. Drag a panel to rotate it and scroll to zoom."
#| echo: false

catalogue_figure = bundled_subunit_figure(catalogue)
catalogue_figure.show(config={
    "displaylogo": False,
    "scrollZoom": True,
    "responsive": True,
})
```

The names and visual gallery are generated from `models/*.pyseb.yaml` during
the documentation build. A newly bundled model appears automatically when it
provides visualization metadata and a validation case containing values for
all structural parameters. The
[Subunit Catalogue](https://github.com/Tobionecenobi/pySEB/wiki/Subunit-Catalogue)
remains the reference for equations, parameters, and reference points.

Three files have different jobs:

| File | Contains | Does not contain |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml` | One subunit's parameters, scattering equations, references, validation cases, and visual geometry | Instances or links |
| `coated-sphere.pyseb-world.yaml` | World ID, model instances, tags, reusable graphs, links, and roots | Parameter values or external model definitions |
| `coated-sphere.usda` | One deterministic visual realization in a chosen length unit | Scattering physics |

Keeping these concerns separate lets one subunit definition serve many worlds,
and one saved world support parameter sweeps and contrast changes.

This tutorial assumes the Python environment from the
[diblock tutorial](diblock-copolymer.qmd). To render its final interactive
OpenUSD figure locally, add the two documentation-only packages:

```bash
python -m pip install plotly usd-core
```

## 1. Write a subunit model

The complete tutorial model is below. It uses the Gaussian-chain scattering
equations, exposes two end references, and asks the visual exporter to draw a
random walk whose radius of gyration is `Rg`.

[Download `FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml`](models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml){download="FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml"}

```yaml
{{< include models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml >}}
```

The scattering expressions and visual geometry share the structural parameter
`Rg`, so a parameter change affects both the calculation and its representative
shape. The random walk is only a visualization of an orientationally averaged
model; it is not used to calculate the form factor.

::: {.callout-note}
The YAML expression language is declarative and restricted. It does not run
Python, C++, shell commands, imports, or arbitrary functions.
:::

## 2. Validate before building

Validation first checks the schema and every expression, then evaluates the
optional numerical reference cases in the file.

```{python}
from pathlib import Path
import tempfile

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np
import pyseb

model_path = Path("models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml").resolve()
report = pyseb.validate_subunit_file(str(model_path))

print("model:", report.model_id)
print("reference cases:", report.case_count)
print("valid:", report.ok)
assert report.ok, [failure.message for failure in report.failures]
```

The equivalent command is useful in continuous integration:

```bash
pyseb-subunit validate models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml
```

It exits with status 0 when the schema and reference cases pass.

## 3. Register and use the model

Registration belongs to one `World`. After registration, either the canonical
ID `tutorial/FlexibleLinker` or the short API name `FlexibleLinker` can be
passed to `Add` and `Link`.

The example attaches twelve user-defined linkers to labelled, deterministic
points on a sphere surface.

```{python}
world = pyseb.World("CustomLinkerTutorial")
model_info = world.register_subunit_file(str(model_path))
print(model_info.id, "registered as", model_info.api_name)

graph = world.Add("SolidSphere", "core")
for index in range(1, 13):
    graph = world.Link(
        "FlexibleLinker",
        f"linker{index}.end1",
        f"core.surface#linker{index}",
    )
world.Add(graph, "coatedSphere")
```

The text after `#` identifies a repeatable representative point on the
distributed sphere surface. With the same instance path and export seed, the
same labels produce the same attachment positions.

For a one-off instance, `world.add_subunit_file(path, name)` loads and adds the
model in one call. `register_subunit_file` is preferable here because the same
model is instantiated repeatedly.

## 4. Supply parameters and evaluate

The custom YAML declares `Rg`; pySEB adds one generated excess-scattering-length
parameter, `beta`, to every scattering subunit. Instance names become parameter
suffixes in the usual way.

```{python}
parameters = {
    "beta_core": 8.0,
    "R_core": 3.0,
}
for index in range(1, 13):
    parameters[f"beta_linker{index}"] = 0.25
    parameters[f"Rg_linker{index}"] = 0.6

q = np.geomspace(1e-3, 2.0, 160)
form_factor = np.asarray(
    world.EvaluateFormFactor("coatedSphere", parameters, q.tolist())
)

print("F(0) =", world.EvaluateFormFactor("coatedSphere", parameters, 0.0))
assert np.isclose(
    world.EvaluateFormFactor("coatedSphere", parameters, 0.0),
    1.0,
)
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-custom-yaml-form-factor
#| fig-cap: "Normalized form factor of a sphere carrying twelve user-defined flexible linkers."

plt.loglog(q, form_factor)
plt.xlabel(r"$q$ (nm$^{-1}$)")
plt.ylabel(r"$F(q)$")
plt.show()
```

## 5. Export and import the world

Use the `.pyseb-world.yaml` format to preserve topology. The tutorial writes
temporary files so rendering the documentation does not leave generated files
in the source tree.

```{python}
temporary_directory = tempfile.TemporaryDirectory()
output_directory = Path(temporary_directory.name)
world_path = output_directory / "coated-sphere.pyseb-world.yaml"

world.save(str(world_path))
print("\n".join(world_path.read_text().splitlines()[:18]))
```

The canonical document records `tutorial/FlexibleLinker` as the model ID. It
does not copy the contents of `FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml` into the world file.
Register that external definition while loading:

```{python}
loaded = pyseb.load_world(
    str(world_path),
    model_files=[str(model_path)],
)

assert world.to_yaml() == loaded.to_yaml()
reloaded_value = loaded.EvaluateFormFactor("coatedSphere", parameters, 0.2)
original_value = world.EvaluateFormFactor("coatedSphere", parameters, 0.2)
assert np.isclose(reloaded_value, original_value)
print(f"round-trip F(0.2) = {reloaded_value:.8f}")
```

For in-memory workflows, use `world.to_yaml()` and
`pyseb.world_from_yaml(yaml_text, model_files=[...])`. The file and string APIs
produce the same canonical YAML.

::: {.callout-important}
World files deliberately omit numerical parameter values. Store fitted or
swept parameter sets separately and pass the selected dictionary to
`Evaluate*` or `export_usd` after loading.
:::

The world CLI validates names, references, graph connectivity, external model
availability, and schema versions without running an analysis:

```bash
pyseb-world validate coated-sphere.pyseb-world.yaml \
  --model-file models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml

pyseb-world inspect coated-sphere.pyseb-world.yaml \
  --model-file models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml
```

`inspect` prints the canonical representation, which is convenient for review
and stable round-trip tests.

## 6. Export a deterministic visual

The YAML model's `visualization` block is consumed by the OpenUSD exporter.
`Readable` layout samples several seeded orientations and relaxes linked
subtrees to improve clearance while preserving every junction.

```{python}
usd_path = output_directory / "coated-sphere.usda"
options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Nanometer)
options.seed = 42
options.layout_mode = pyseb.LayoutMode.Readable
options.orientation_trials = 32
options.relaxation_sweeps = 2
options.surface_samples = 40
options.curve_samples = 48
options.color_overrides = {
    "core": (0.18, 0.48, 0.78),
    **{
        f"linker{index}": (0.92, 0.42, 0.14)
        for index in range(1, 13)
    },
}
options.opacity_overrides = {"core": 0.62}

loaded.export_usd(
    "coatedSphere",
    str(usd_path),
    parameters,
    options,
)

print(usd_path.name, f"({usd_path.stat().st_size / 1024:.1f} KiB)")
print("\n".join(usd_path.read_text().splitlines()[:8]))
```

The text USDA file opens in Blender, `usdview`, and other OpenUSD tools; pySEB
does not require an OpenUSD runtime to write it. The seed makes the
representative random walks, distributed attachment positions, and layout
repeatable. Change it when you want another equally valid realization.

The documentation build can now open that exact USDA file with the OpenUSD
Python bindings and hand its resolved meshes and curves to Plotly. This adapter
lives in `docs/tutorials/_helpers.py`; it is not part of pySEB's runtime API or
required dependencies.

```{python}
#| label: fig-interactive-openusd
#| fig-cap: "Interactive realization read back from the OpenUSD file produced above."

from _helpers import usd_to_plotly

interactive_scene = usd_to_plotly(usd_path)
interactive_scene.show(config={
    "displaylogo": False,
    "scrollZoom": True,
    "responsive": True,
})
```

Drag to orbit, scroll to zoom, and hover over geometry to see its resolved USD
path. Python and OpenUSD run during the documentation build; the published page
loads Plotly's JavaScript renderer to handle interaction in the browser.

## C++ equivalents

The same files are portable to the C++ API. Include the world parser explicitly
for import and export:

```cpp
#include "SEB.hpp"
#include "WorldIO/WorldParser.hpp"

World world("CustomLinkerTutorial");
world.RegisterSubunitFile("models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml");
GraphID graph = world.Add("SolidSphere", "core");
graph = world.Link(
    "FlexibleLinker", "linker1.end1", "core.surface#linker1");
world.Add(graph, "coatedSphere");

pyseb::SaveWorld(world, "coated-sphere.pyseb-world.yaml");
auto loaded = pyseb::LoadWorld(
    "coated-sphere.pyseb-world.yaml",
    {"models/FlexibleLinker.pyseb.yaml"});

ParameterList parameters{
    {"R_core", 3.0},
    {"Rg_linker1", 0.6},
};
USDExportOptions options(LengthUnit::Nanometer);
options.seed = 42;
options.layoutMode = USDLayoutMode::Readable;
loaded->ExportUSD(
    "coatedSphere", "coated-sphere.usda", parameters, options);
```

`AddFile` and `LinkFile` are the C++ one-off loading conveniences corresponding
to Python's `add_subunit_file` and `link_subunit_file`.

## What else is new in 0.3.0?

- YAML models can define reusable one-dimensional or ordered iterated finite
  integrals with CQUAD or QAG. Use them for orientational averages that do not
  have a closed form.
- `sinc` and `jinc` provide stable removable limits at zero, and the expression
  language also includes Bessel, Struve, Dawson, and error functions.
- Visual references support fixed positions, curve fractions, distributed
  sampling, labelled identities, and named variants such as opposite cylinder
  caps or spheroid poles.
- OpenUSD export supports random or best-effort readable layouts, per-instance
  colors and opacity, custom length units, and visualization-only envelopes for
  Debye sphere clouds.
- Bundled analytic models are now discovered from YAML. Construct catalogue
  models through `World.Add()` and `World.Link()`; direct constructors are not
  available for YAML-backed entries.

The [file-defined subunit guide](../file-defined-subunits.qmd) documents the
complete schema and integral rules. The
[visualization guide](../visualization.qmd) covers geometry patches, layout
controls, named variants, Debye envelopes, and the example gallery.
